interest: This file offers a unique look at the intersection of international environmental conservation and post-World War II diplomatic planning for the Japanese Peace Treaty. It demonstrates how prominent conservationists like Ira N. Gabrielson, former director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, liaised directly with the State Department's International Resources Division to advocate for the protection of trans-Pacific wildlife. The documents provide valuable historical context on early transnational ecological awareness regarding North Pacific and Bering Sea migratory flyways, specifically highlighting species such as the Emperor Goose and various pelagic seabirds.
overview: This file contains correspondence and a memorandum of conversation from September and October 1947 concerning wildlife conservation provisions for the post-World War II peace treaty with Japan, classified under decimal file 894.6232 (wild animals, game laws, and birds). The documents record exchanges between Dr. Ira N. Gabrielson, President of the Wildlife Management Institute, and William E. S. Flory of the State Department's International Resources Division. Gabrielson evaluates the necessity of including treaty protections for migratory and pelagic bird species that cross the North Pacific between North America and Japan—particularly the Emperor Goose breeding in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and wintering in the Aleutians and Japan, as well as various pelagic seabirds in the Bering Sea.

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum recording a conversation with Ira N. Gabrielson concerning migratory bird protection provisions in the proposed Japanese Peace Treaty.
subfiles.from: William E. S. Flory (International Resources Division, Department of State)
subfiles.summary: William E. S. Flory of the State Department's International Resources Division documents a discussion with Dr. Ira N. Gabrielson, President of the Wildlife Management Institute, regarding wildlife protection clauses in the proposed Japanese treaty. Gabrielson raised concerns over whether the treaty would secure protection in Japan for migratory birds covered under the U.S.-Canada Migratory Bird Treaty, specifically noting the Emperor Goose which breeds in the Yukon Delta and winters in the Aleutian Islands and Japan. The memorandum also notes similar migration and wintering patterns for pelagic species such as puffins, murres, auklets, murrelets, and gulls.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Wildlife Protection in the Japanese Treaty

subfiles.about: A letter from Ira N. Gabrielson advising the State Department on the extent to which pelagic and migratory birds require treaty protection in Japanese waters and the Bering Sea.
subfiles.from: Ira N. Gabrielson (President, Wildlife Management Institute)
subfiles.summary: Dr. Ira N. Gabrielson replies to William E. S. Flory regarding the inclusion of wildlife conservation measures in the prospective Japanese peace treaty alongside provisions for fur seals and pelagic fisheries. Gabrielson explains that few bird species cross hemispheres, identifying the Emperor Goose from the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta area as the primary species crossing from Alaska to Japan and the Asiatic coast. He observes that while Japanese fishing boats historically harvested some pelagic birds in the Bering Sea and Aleutians, the harvest was negligible; nevertheless, he suggests including protective provisions for pelagic and migratory birds in areas adjacent to the Bering Sea.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ira N. Gabrielson to William E. S. Flory regarding Pelagic and Migratory Bird Protection
